post: The road to the Constitution begins with a printing press. Why did Mary Katharine Goddard risk placing her own name beneath the Declaration of Independence? How did Mercy Otis Warren bring revolutionary ideas into the homes of everyday Americans? In the first video from BRIs Constitution Day 2026 programming, discover how 2 women used ink, information, and courage to help citizens understand independence and prepare for the responsibilities of self-government. History looks inevitable only in hindsight. BRI Director of Communications Lindsay Moran shares how a living-room debate sparked by Young Washington became a lesson in historical perspective: understanding not only what people chose, but what they knew, believed, and risked when they made that choice. That kind of inquiry is at the heart of history and civics education. It asks students to examine evidence, question assumptions, and understand the past before deciding what they think about it. For more on how to inspire young thinkers using the film, check out BRI's resources exploring the life and times of George Washington:  https://lnkd.in/gzcH4kjd Big thanks to Daniels Fund for helping make these resources possible.  #YoungWashington  #HistoryEducation  #CivicsEducation

I was watching Young Washington (again!) with my boyfriend when he casually announced: "Yeah, if Id been alive then, I probably would have been on the side of the British.  Whaaaaaat? (He might as well have told me he cheated on ME.) How can you even SAY that?  I demanded. He calmly explained that if he had actually been a young man living in the colonies at the time it probably wouldnt have occurred to him that British rule was something to overthrow. The revolutionaries would have seemed like radicals. I was having none of it. "Nope. Not me. I would have been with the Americans!  Maybe not on the battlefield. But definitely in spirit. (Possibly as a spy. 🤔 ) But then, annoyingly, I started to realize he had a point. We love to - or at least I love to - imagine that if we had lived at some pivotal moment in history, we know exactly what we would have done. We would have recognized the right side immediately. We would have been brave. We would have questioned assumptions everyone else took for granted. But of course, we know how the story ends. The people living it didn't. Even George Washington spent his early adulthood fighting on Britain's side in the French and Indian War. He served alongside British forces and actually wanted a commission in the regular British Army but the higher-ups repeatedly said no. This man who would eventually command the entire Continental Army didn't start out knowing that was where history, or even his own convictions, would take him. That's what stayed with me after our "argument." History gets flattened when we look backward. Choices seem obvious because we already know which ideas prevailed and which causes succeeded. Living through history, as each of us does every day, is different. It's messy and uncertain. People make decisions based on incomplete information (nowadays sometimes mis- or disinformation), personal interests, assumptions and biases, greed, fear, courage, whatever . . . not to mention NO idea what the next chapter is going to say. One thing I love about my job at BRI is that I'm encountering questions like this every day. Not simply, What happened? but Why did people make the choices they made? What did the world look like from where they were standing? And what might we have done if we'd been standing there too? Those questions make history a lot more interesting to me, and a little more humbling. (Still . . . pretty sure I would have been a Patriot spy 😎 )

It started with questions grandparents ask their grandchildren every day. How do I send a text? How do I fix the volume on this thing? Medha and Reshma Lalani could have answered and moved on. Instead they recognized something larger behind the questions: a digital divide separating an entire generation from the tools modern life now requires. So they built Tech Buddies, connecting high school students with seniors for personalized, 1-on-1 tech help. The initiative has now reached more than 3,500 seniors and grown to over 115 student volunteers, with new chapters forming internationally. This is what civic virtue looks like when a students put it into practice. Responsibility, in seeing a need and claiming it. Respect, in affirming the dignity of people left behind in our rapidly changing world. Meet the 2026 MyImpact Challenge National Grand Prize Winners and hear the story in their own words, alongside a moving reflection from the grandparents who inspired it. 👉  https://bit.ly/3U9e1Ae  #MyImpactChallenge  #CivicsEducation  #StudentLeadership  #CivicVirtue  #BRI

The Founders understood rights as protections. No one may interfere with your speech, your worship, your property. Franklin Roosevelt proposed something different: rights the government must actively provide. His 1944 State of the Union, the "Second Bill of Rights" speech, listed employment, medical care, housing, and economic security among them. Roosevelt died 15 months later, but his successors passed much of the agenda into law. The distinction between negative and positive rights is one of the most consequential ideas in American constitutional debate, and it remains genuinely contested today. BRI's newest Primary Source Essentials makes that distinction clear in just a couple of minutes. Watch it here:  https://bit.ly/4zb2Yq9  #CivicEducation  #AmericanHistory  #PrimarySources  #ConstitutionalPrinciples

John Adams thought Americans would celebrate independence on July 2. That was the day the Second Continental Congress unanimously adopted Richard Henry Lee's resolution declaring the colonies "free and independent states." Adams wrote to Abigail that it was the greatest question ever debated in America. 2 days later, Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence, and July 4 became the date we remember. Both days mattered. Understanding why is the beginning of understanding what the Declaration actually did. BRI's newest A250 Mini Documentary walks through the full sequence: the debate, the drafting, and the principles of equality, natural rights, and self-government that Americans have been claiming ever since. Watch it here:  https://bit.ly/45qL59g  #CivicEducation  #AmericanHistory  #A250  #DeclarationOfIndependence

Amber Chih grew up with Tourette syndrome. So she built something to make sure people like her are heard. The Northwood High School student just won the $7,500 grand prize in BRI's MyImpact Challenge for A Thousand Words, an advocacy program amplifying the voices of people with invisible disabilities. She interviewed 50+ people across America, built a storytelling gallery, created a classroom curriculum that's reached 2,500+ students, and partnered with the City of Irvine to launch Invisible Disabilities Awareness Week. Fellow Irvine student Shaili Chudasama of Portola High School took the $5,000 second prize for Startup Stars, teaching 100+ middle schoolers to launch real businesses. This is what happens when students turn personal passion into community impact. Congratulations to both 👇  https://bit.ly/4wmci89  #CivicEducation  #StudentLeadership  #MyImpactChallenge  #Civics
